newsitem.title: BULGARIA: NEW BULGARIAN PRESIDENT WANTS ELECTIONS, REFORMS.
newsitem.headline: NEW BULGARIAN PRESIDENT WANTS ELECTIONS, REFORMS.

text.p: Bulgarian President Petar Stoyanov has called on the ruling Socialists to accept demands for quick elections by returning the mandate he will give them on Tuesday to try to form a new government.

"For almost a month Bulgaria has been in a deep crisis. It is on the threshhold of hyperinflation. Immediate political and financial stabilisation is needed to survive the winter," said Stoyanov, who was sworn in as president last week.
Bulgaria has been in political limbo since Socialist prime minister Zhan Videnov and his cabinet resigned on December 21.
Stoyanov, a lawyer and pro-market liberal, said he wanted to name an interim government and hold a special 10-day session of parliament to adopt vital economic reforms.
"Bulgaria needs very fast reforms because payments on domestic and foreign debt are due and the most important of them is due in July," he said in his statement to reporters.

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has withheld a 115 million standby credit because the Socialists failed to carry out reforms, such as closing loss-making state companies and speeding up privatisation.

The Balkan state has been swept into crisis with inflation now above 300 percent annually, the lev driven down to record lows and protesters packing Sofia's streets daily to call for immediate elections.
The demonstrators, who plan a 23rd day of street protests on Tuesday, fiercely oppose the Socialists staying in power.

Under the constitution, Stoyanov must give the mandate to the Socialists first, as the largest party in parliament. If they fail to form a government, the mandate will be offered in turn to each of the opposition parties.
If they all fail, elections will be held within two months. Stoyanov asked all parties to return the mandate immediately to speed elections -- not due until December 1998.

Wheeling and dealing was expected throughout the night. The Socialists have an absolute majority in the 240-seat parliament but they are divided between reform-minded social democrats and hardline opponents to change.
Opposition parties have vowed to intensify their protests if the Socialists form a new government and the country could be plunged into a prolonged economic crisis.
"I will hand the mandate with a clear mind that if now we miss the chance for a political compromise, the crisis will not be overcome," Stoyanov said.
While he has negotiated between the Socialists and the opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDR), anti-government protests have continued and the lev has been in a freefall.
"People are getting poorer by the hour and that is why they are in the street demonstrating," said Viktor Papazov, chairman of the Bulgarian Stock Exchange.
Some 2,000 students with white-painted faces held a "march of the dead" in Sofia on Monday, blowing whistles and shaking cans full of worthless levs.
They joined some 18,000 protesters at an opposition rally at Alexander Nevsky cathedral, including a group of miners with helmets and lamps.
"I'm here because I'm hungry and I'm angry," proclaimed one banner.
